solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Set up clubs supported by important individual

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit
a thing resting on another is supported by it
a leading figure is an important person

explanation.surface: A golf or social club being established with the backing of some notable patron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supported by' is the charade glue: clubs sits on the figure, which is how ON enters.
explanation.definitionFit: To configure a system is to arrange or establish it, the same meaning as putting something in place and getting it ready.

clue.text: Humorous ridicule which affronted nurses

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the phrase cradles the letters wanted inside it

parts.note: taken from the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Teasing that offended the nurses on a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like hospital staff but is a verb meaning holds; the answer spans the join between two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaff as a noun is light-hearted banter or teasing, good-natured mockery exchanged between friends.

clue.text: Complex number precedes zero

parts.note: NO is the standard abbreviation for number
a complex, as in an obsession, is a 'thing' someone has about something

explanation.surface: A maths statement: a complex number comes before zero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex number' reads as the mathematical term, but the words split: complex is a noun meaning a hang-up, and 'precedes' puts NO first.
explanation.definitionFit: Nothing and zero both denote an absence of any quantity, as in the score being nothing or nil.

clue.text: Maiden's promise hampered by endless exams

indicators.note: without ends means both the first and last letters are cut away
something hampered is hemmed in on both sides by what obstructs it

parts.note: FINALS, the last university exams, with first and last letters removed
to augur well is to promise well, to bode

explanation.surface: A young woman's pledge is held back by exams that never seem to end.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay. Finals are the final-year university exams.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden speech or voyage is the first of its kind, and inaugural likewise describes an opening or first occasion.

clue.text: Fanatical airmen deployed overseas

indicators.note: troops deployed are spread out into new positions, so the letters are redistributed

parts.note: an ultra is an extremist, and ultra- means extreme
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Zealous RAF crews sent abroad on active service.
explanation.walkthrough: Ultramarine is mostly known as a blue pigment, but its older, literal sense is 'beyond the sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin ultra means beyond and marinus of the sea, so ultramarine literally describes places situated abroad across the ocean.

clue.text: Use heroin regularly for a long time

indicators.note: at regular intervals means taking every second letter in turn

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: An addict's long-term habit of taking heroin over years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use' just sets the scene: the even letters of the drug's name give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An eon is an immensely long period, an age, so it serves as a noun for a very extended stretch.

clue.text: Note duplicated carbon copy

parts.note: MI is the third note of the sol-fa scale, written twice
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: An office memo copied twice over with carbon paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carbon copy' reads as one phrase, but carbon belongs to the wordplay and copy alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To mimic someone is to imitate them, reproducing their manner as a copy does its original.

clue.text: Way of working involving a large number of bits and sequence of steps

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one element enfolds the others

parts.note: MO is modus operandi, a way of working
taken as written
MB, a megabit, is a million bits

explanation.surface: A computing procedure handling lots of data and a series of instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all computing jargon; 'sequence of steps' turns out to mean dance steps.
explanation.definitionFit: The mambo is a Cuban ballroom dance, and any dance is a set routine of footwork patterns.

clue.text: Damage can start to impair it?

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
a tin is a can

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: opening letter

explanation.surface: Could a dent in the can spoil its contents?
explanation.walkthrough: In 'gin and it', 'it' is Italian vermouth; Martini is a famous brand of it, hence the question mark for a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian vermouth is called 'it' in British bars, and Martini is a well-known brand of that Italian vermouth.

clue.text: Partner institution welcomes a university accepting teaching ultimately

indicators.note: to welcome is to take guests inside, so one element lets another in
to accept is to take in, so one element receives another within it

parts.note: a college is an educational institution
taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university
the last letter of this word is the G already in the institution, which the two inserted letters straddle

explanation.surface: A partner college hosts a university to boost its teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: A and U go into COLLEGE either side of its G, so A-G-U reads as 'a university accepting' the G that ends teaching; the setter lets that G do double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A colleague is someone you work alongside, a fellow in a profession, which is what a partner in business is.

clue.text: Draw cover for anti-racist leaflet

indicators.note: a cover wraps the outside, so only the outermost letters are wanted

parts.note: first and last letters
a tract is a pamphlet or leaflet

explanation.surface: Designing the front page of a campaign pamphlet against racism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests sketching a cover design, but it is the verb meaning pull in.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a crowd is to attract it, both meaning pull people or things towards you.

clue.text: What may symbolise one rule man breaks

indicators.note: something that breaks falls apart, so its letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A symbol for a person who flouts the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' suggests a person; it is the number one, which the figure 1 or Roman I stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: A numeral is a written figure standing for a number, and one such figure represents the number one.

clue.text: Shy couple's brief relationship

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to throw, as at a coconut shy
second meaning: a short-lived romantic affair

explanation.surface: A bashful pair whose romance does not last long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid, but it is the verb meaning throw; a coconut shy is a fairground stall where balls are thrown at coconuts.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as a verb for hurling something and as a noun for a short casual love affair.

clue.text: Solitary TV presenter cut short piece

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its tail, the final letter

parts.note: a news anchor presents a programme
ITEM, a piece in a news bulletin, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A lone newsreader whose report was trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solitary' looks like an adjective but is a noun here: a solitary is a hermit.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchorite is a religious recluse who lives shut away from society, and a solitary is such a hermit.

clue.text: Docking terminal moved within canal

indicators.note: within places one thing inside the other
things moved are shifted around from their original places

parts.note: these eight letters rearranged
a cut is a canal in British usage

explanation.surface: A ship berthing at a terminal that has been relocated inside a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docking' suggests boats at a terminal on a canal, but it means cutting short, as a tail is docked.
explanation.definitionFit: Docking pay or a tail means reducing it, and curtailment is the act of cutting something back.

clue.text: Tiresome activity removing length of cloth as standard

indicators.note: removing means taking something out and leaving the rest

parts.note: a standard is a cloth banner, a flag
L is the abbreviation for length, taken out

explanation.surface: A dull job cutting a length of fabric to a standard size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of cloth as' qualifies the standard: a flag is a standard made of cloth. In British slang a fag is a chore, a tedious task.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal usage calls a wearisome chore a fag, as in 'what a fag', meaning an irksome bother.

clue.text: Experience — the best preparation for features

parts.note: to face something is to undergo or experience it
the cream is the best of anything

explanation.surface: A motto: experience is the finest training for what lies ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preparation' reads as getting ready, but it is a cosmetic product, and 'features' are the parts of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmetic preparation is a lotion or product, and face cream is one applied to the facial features.

clue.text: Parent organised engagement around name changing

indicators.note: around places one thing so it encircles another

parts.note: to parent a child is to rear it
to run an event is to organise it
a gig is a musician's booking, an engagement
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A mother or father plans a wedding engagement around the switch of surname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised' looks like an anagram signal and 'engagement' like a betrothal, but they are RAN and a musician's booking.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearranging means altering the order or layout of something, so it is a form of changing it.

clue.text: I turn bananas into processed food

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims to turn bananas into factory-made food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit being processed, but it is the signal, and 'into' is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutrition is nourishment, food as the body takes in and digests it, which is food being processed.

clue.text: Grumble about state briefly wishing to please

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a grumble is a complaint
SA is the abbreviation for South Australia, an Australian state

explanation.surface: Moaning about the state of things while trying to be agreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: The grumble is a noun here, not a verb. Don't confuse the answer with complacent, which sounds similar.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaisant describes someone obliging and eager to accommodate others, keen to go along and be agreeable.

clue.text: Piece of music is heard to a greater extent

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by ear, so its sound matters rather than its spelling

parts.note: 'more so' means to a greater degree

explanation.surface: A musical composition becomes louder or more prominent.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for a morsel is borrowed in English for a short musical piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A morceau is a short composition or passage, a brief musical work, taken from French for a bit.

clue.text: Anticipated means of obtaining satisfaction fails to reach conclusion

indicators.note: falling short of the finish leaves a word with its tail end lopped off

parts.note: DUEL, the gentleman's way of demanding satisfaction, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: An expected route to contentment never quite pays off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Satisfaction' reads as contentment, but it is the old sense of redress for an insult, won in a duel.
explanation.definitionFit: Something due is expected or scheduled to arrive, as in a train due at noon, so it is awaited.

clue.text: Misrepresent policeman's reason for seeking compensation

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector, plus the S of the possessive
a tort is a civil wrong for which damages can be claimed

explanation.surface: A police officer's grounds for suing someone, twisted for effect.
explanation.walkthrough: Tort is the legal term for a civil wrong giving grounds for a damages claim.
explanation.definitionFit: To distort facts is to twist them so they give a false impression, which is misrepresenting them.

clue.text: Company initially recognising China controls mineral material

indicators.note: to control is to hold in check, so one piece holds another

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter alone

parts.note: opening letter
china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, so china is a pal
ore is a mineral from which metal is extracted

explanation.surface: A firm that first acknowledged China now controls the mineral supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but it is rhyming slang: china plate = mate, i.e. a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means bodily or physical, having substance, which is what material means as an adjective.

clue.text: Bulb working with electricity generator

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
ions are charged particles whose movement produces electric current

explanation.surface: A light bulb that lights up when powered by a generator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' suggests a lamp, but it is the vegetable kind grown underground.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion is the swollen underground storage organ of a plant, which botanists call a bulb.

clue.text: Children's lives pursue action

parts.note: to live is to exist, and 'is' also means exists
to sue is to pursue a legal action

explanation.surface: Kids' lives are about getting on with doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is' as a link; 'action' is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a formal and legal word for offspring, as in 'died without issue', meaning descendants.

clue.text: Revise pieces penned by journalist

indicators.note: animals penned are shut inside an enclosure

parts.note: ED is short for editor
chess pieces are called men

explanation.surface: An editor revising articles written by a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces' suggests articles and 'penned' writing; instead they are chessmen, shut inside the editor.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct and improve it, so it is a precise synonym of revising writing.

clue.text: Levelling up happening late in the day

definitions.meaning: first meaning: making equal, as a team does with the score
second meaning: describing something in the late part of the day

explanation.surface: A political slogan about narrowing regional gaps, coming rather late on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Levelling up' sounds like UK regional policy, but it is the participle of 'even up'; the answer is pronounced differently in each sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening up means making level, and the adjective evening describes events at the day's close, as in evening classes.

clue.text: Man with outstanding physique died after game

parts.note: Go is a Japanese board game
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A bodybuilder passes away after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts D behind the game. A muscular hunk is informally called a Greek god.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a handsome muscular man a god, as in 'Greek god', praises his splendid build and looks.

clue.text: Abridgement of large-scale literary volume?

parts.note: surface reading: a shortened version of a big book
setter's reading: an epic tome, which with one letter dropped from its middle becomes a word for a summary

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the play: the word looks like 'epic tome' abridged by losing its C, and it really does mean a summary.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome, in its older sense, is a condensed summary or abstract of a longer written work.

clue.text: Keen reporter's start to the day

indicators.note: a reporter speaks aloud, so what matters is how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: morn is the start of the day, morning

explanation.surface: An eager journalist beginning the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like eager, but it is the verb meaning to wail in grief. The two words sound alike in non-rhotic British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to lament loudly over the dead, an Irish tradition of wailing grief, which is to mourn.

clue.text: Blew up school with unfashionable exterior

indicators.note: an exterior is an outer shell, so one piece forms the outside of another

parts.note: dated means out of fashion
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Someone bombed a school whose outside was drab and old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blew up' could be a temper, but here it is an explosion. Eton College is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate is to set off an explosive, and something detonated has exploded or burst apart.
